analysis.one_liner: Requires TV drug ads to show the drug's list price on screen.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with support from both parties, has not moved since being referred to two House committees in July 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the federal agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid to write a rule requiring TV ads for prescription drugs covered by those programs to display the drug's list price — the price for a typical 30-day supply — as text on screen. The idea is that people seeing a drug advertised would also see what it costs. The agency could decide to extend the requirement to other kinds of ads and to add enforcement rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries and anyone shopping for or negotiating over an advertised drug, who would see the list price every time the drug is advertised on television. Advertising is one of the main ways drugmakers reach patients directly, and today those ads generally do not state what the drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: Within a year of enactment, federal regulators would have to require that TV ads (broadcast, cable, streaming, and satellite) for drugs paid for by Medicare or Medicaid display a truthful statement of the drug's list price for a typical 30-day regimen or course of treatment, priced as of the first day of the quarter the ad airs. [S3]
The rule would cover television specifically, including streaming, which is where a growing share of drug advertising reaches viewers. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drugmakers, whose ads would have to carry a price and whose marketing might become less persuasive when a $1,000-a-month drug shows its price on screen. Television broadcasters and cable networks could also see less drug-ad revenue if ads shrink.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires disclosure, not lower prices. Showing a list price does not change what a patient actually pays at the pharmacy, which depends on insurance design and the hidden discounts that pharmacy benefit managers negotiate. A viewer may see a list price far higher than anyone's real out-of-pocket cost. [S3]

The bill covers only drugs for which Medicare or Medicaid payment is available and only television ads; the agency would have to decide separately whether to extend the rule to other forms of advertising, so many ads a consumer actually sees could remain unpriced. [S3]
Enforcement mechanisms, ad format, and whether other price information must be shown are all left to the agency to work out, so the practical strength of the requirement is uncertain. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: viewers would get a basic fact — the list price — that drug ads currently omit, and that could help patients ask better questions and push back. It would not by itself lower anyone's drug bill, and the gap between the list price shown and what people actually pay could confuse as much as inform. A well-designed disclosure rule is a reasonable, low-cost step; a badly designed one is a number on a screen that matches nothing on a receipt.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees in July 2025, and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Nikema Williams of Georgia introduced the bill on July 22, 2025, joined by Reps. Don Bacon, Angie Craig, and Bryan Steil as original cosponsors. [S1][S3]
The bill has 4 cosponsors — 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat. [S4]
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, markup, or floor vote. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything: drugmakers keep advertising without showing prices, and patients keep paying without a visible price. The bill's small bipartisan group of sponsors has nothing to show for it yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drugmakers, so far — no rules changed

for.name: Nikema Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring TV drug ads to display list prices.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and the cosponsor list splits 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat; no opposition has been recorded, and the bill has simply not advanced out of committee.

industries.note: Drugmakers would have to print a truthful list price on TV ads for Medicare- and Medicaid-covered drugs, which could make ads less persuasive and give patients a talking point against high prices. The industry's interest in keeping prices out of its advertising runs directly against consumers' interest in seeing them.

Pharmaceutical advertising is a major revenue source, and the bill does not ban or restrict the ads themselves — but if a price on screen makes ads less effective, drugmakers may buy less airtime. Networks' interest runs with drugmakers' here.

The bill does not touch them directly, but showing list prices highlights the gap between list prices and the negotiated prices these middlemen produce — attention their business model does not invite.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to two committees (Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means) with no action since introduction. With 4 cosponsors and no hearing or markup scheduled, the likely path — as for most House bills at this stage — is that it stays in committee for the rest of the Congress unless its sponsors build much broader support or attach the idea to larger legislation.
